RagShortTexts: The ruling elite of Vandals comprised ancient aristocratic houses and military dynasties competing for feudal land and fiscal control.
Domestic politics were profoundly steered by court intrigues and noble factions resisting excessive central centralization.
Intricate matrimonial alliances and blood feuds permeated the nobility, ensuring that disputed successions frequently sparked nationwide crises.

Variants.Content: Within the opulent halls and sprawling feudal estates of Vandals, the balance of domestic power remained in perilous equilibrium. Ancient lineages commanded vast agricultural latifundia, hereditary warrior retinues, and lucrative trade monopolies, acting simultaneously as imperial cornerstones and covert rivals to the throne. Court assemblies seethed with venomous factionalism, pitting entrenched senatorial aristocrats against battle-hardened military commanders who demanded greater political dominance. Behind tapestried corridors, clandestine poisonings, forged wills, and intercepted treaties dictated political ascendancy. Lesser vassals maneuvered cautiously between dominant magnates, ready to shift allegiance whenever the central authority showed signs of exhaustion or military defeat.

Inside the hall, two magnates are shouting over mine leases, and a silver goblet has just struck the floor. Guardsmen at the door stare at the far wall. If the feud spills into the courtyard, the common men with spears will die first, while the quarrelling houses sit safely behind their tables.

The elder of the house calls his heir to the study and sets a wax tablet between them. Thrones pass away, he says, but the castles and serf villages must be kept whole. Greet rival barons with courtesy, count your armed men quietly, and send no letter naming a faction until you know which way the wind will blow.
